hints: Notice the spring initially supports both masses, $0.20\text{ kg}$ plus $0.10\text{ kg}$, so find the spring force from static equilibrium before cutting.
Recall the spring extension cannot change instantly, so immediately after the thread is cut the upward spring force is still equal to the combined weight.
Connect the unbalanced force on the $0.20\text{ kg}$ mass to $F = ma$: subtract its own weight from that unchanged spring force, then divide by $0.20\text{ kg}$.
walkthrough: In static equilibrium before cutting, resultant force is zero, so upward spring force $F_s$ equals total downward weight: $F_s = (0.20 + 0.10)g = 0.30g$.
With $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$, $F_s = 0.30 \times 9.81 = 2.943\text{ N}$ upward on the $0.20\text{ kg}$ mass.
Immediately after the thread is cut the spring length is unchanged, so $F_s$ is still $2.943\text{ N}$ upward, but the downward pull of the $0.10\text{ kg}$ mass is removed.
For the $0.20\text{ kg}$ mass alone, weight is $W = 0.20g = 0.20 \times 9.81 = 1.962\text{ N}$ downward.
Net upward force is $F_{net} = F_s - W = 2.943 - 1.962 = 0.981\text{ N}$, which equals the removed $0.10g$ weight.
Use $F_{net} = ma$: $a = F_{net}/m = 0.981/0.20 = 4.905\text{ m s}^{-2}$ upward, about $4.9\text{ m s}^{-2}$. This is option A.

options.A: Net upward force is $0.10g$ so $a = 0.10g/0.20 = 0.5g = 4.9\text{ m s}^{-2}$ upward.
options.B: This incorrectly divides the unbalanced $0.10g$ force by the total $0.30\text{ kg}$ instead of by the $0.20\text{ kg}$ that remains on the spring.
options.C: This is $g$, which would need a net force equal to the full weight of the $0.20\text{ kg}$ mass, not the $0.10g$ excess spring force.
options.D: This divides the full pre-cut spring force $0.30g$ by $0.20\text{ kg}$ and ignores the downward weight of the $0.20\text{ kg}$ mass.
